name: Colosseum, Rome
summary: Flavian Amphitheatre in central Rome, completed under Emperor Titus in 80 AD.
presentContext: A global cultural icon and UNESCO World Heritage site, visited by over 7 million people annually. Ongoing preservation battles weather erosion and subway vibrations.

facts.claim: Construction began under the emperor Vespasian in 72 AD and was completed in 80 AD under Titus.
facts.supportingExcerpt: Construction of the Colosseum was begun between 70 and 72 CE during the reign of Vespasian and completed in 80 CE under Titus.

facts.claim: It could hold an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators and was used for gladiatorial contests and public spectacles.
facts.sourceTitle: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Historic Centre of Rome
facts.supportingExcerpt: The monumental amphitheatre could accommodate tens of thousands of Roman spectators for civic games.

facts.claim: In medieval times, the structure was repurposed as housing, workshops, quarters for a religious order, and a fortress.
facts.supportingExcerpt: By the late 6th century a small chapel had been built into the structure... converted into housing and workshops.

facts.claim: Major damage occurred from the 1349 earthquake, after which fallen stone was reused to construct palazzi and churches.
facts.sourceTitle: Encyclopaedia Britannica — The Great Earthquake of 1349
facts.supportingExcerpt: The Colosseum was severely damaged by the great earthquake of 1349, causing the outer south side to collapse.

images.caption: The Colosseum under evening light in Rome.

name: Machu Picchu, Cusco
summary: 15th-century Inca citadel situated on an Andean mountain ridge at 2,430 metres.
presentContext: Peru's most renowned archaeological sanctuary, regulated with strict daily visitor quotas to protect fragile dry-stone terraces against tectonic instability and mass tourism.

facts.claim: Constructed around 1450 CE at the height of the Inca Empire under Pachacuti.
facts.sourceTitle: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu
facts.supportingExcerpt: Machu Picchu was built in the fifteenth century and abandoned when the Inca Empire was conquered by the Spaniards.

facts.claim: Built with dry-stone walls made of polished ashlar granite stones fitted together without mortar.
facts.supportingExcerpt: The masonry is mortarless cut-stone construction, typical of the finest Inca architecture.

facts.claim: Brought to international academic attention in 1911 by American historian and explorer Hiram Bingham.
facts.sourceTitle: National Geographic — Lost City of the Incas
facts.supportingExcerpt: In 1911, Hiram Bingham III of Yale University climbed the ridge and documented the site.

images.caption: Terraces and stone ruins overlooking the Urubamba valley.

name: Parthenon, Athens
summary: Former temple on the Athenian Acropolis dedicated to the goddess Athena, completed in 438 BC.
presentContext: The focal monument of the Acropolis of Athens, undergoing meticulous restoration using rescued Pentelic marble and advanced robotic stonemasonry.

facts.claim: Constructed between 447 and 432 BC under the political leadership of Pericles, with Phidias supervising artistic decor.
facts.supportingExcerpt: The Parthenon was built under the leadership of Pericles between 447 and 432 BCE.

facts.claim: Conducted service as an Athenian treasury and later converted into a Christian church in the 6th century AD.
facts.sourceTitle: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Acropolis, Athens
facts.supportingExcerpt: In the Byzantine period, the Parthenon was turned into a church dedicated to the Virgin Mary.

facts.claim: In 1687, an Ottoman ammunition depot inside the building ignited during a Venetian siege, causing immense structural collapse.
facts.supportingExcerpt: The Venetian bombardment under Morosini ignited gunpowder stored in the temple on September 26, 1687.

images.caption: The Doric columns of the Parthenon atop the Acropolis.

name: Angkor Wat, Siem Reap
summary: Vast temple complex and hydraulic landscape built by King Suryavarman II in the early 12th century.
presentContext: Heart of Cambodia's national identity, featured on its national flag. International teams collaborate on water management systems to stabilize subsoil foundations.

facts.claim: Originally founded as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu by Khmer King Suryavarman II in the first half of the 12th century.
facts.supportingExcerpt: Angkor Wat was built by King Suryavarman II in the early 12th century as a state temple and eventual mausoleum.

facts.claim: Gradually transformed into a Buddhist pilgrimage site by the late 12th century, retaining its religious function over centuries.
facts.supportingExcerpt: Toward the end of the 12th century, it gradually transformed into a Buddhist centre of worship.

facts.claim: Encircled by an expansive 190-meter-wide moat and integrated into a sophisticated hydraulic reservoir network.
facts.sourceTitle: Smithsonian Magazine — Secrets of Angkor Hydraulic Engineering
facts.supportingExcerpt: A giant rectangular moat surrounded the temple, acting as both spiritual boundary and hydraulic stabilizing foundation.

images.caption: Angkor Wat towers reflecting across the central pond.

name: Taj Mahal, Agra
summary: Ivory-white marble mausoleum on the southern bank of the Yamuna River, commissioned in 1631 by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan.
presentContext: A jewel of Indo-Islamic architecture attracting millions of travelers. Strict eco-zones regulate industrial air emissions in Agra to protect the translucent Makrana marble.

facts.claim: Commissioned by Shah Jahan in 1631 to house the tomb of his favourite wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
facts.sourceTitle: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Taj Mahal
facts.supportingExcerpt: An immense mausoleum of white marble, built in Agra between 1631 and 1648 by order of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan.

facts.claim: Chief architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori oversaw an artisan guild numbering more than 20,000 workers and 1,000 elephants.
facts.supportingExcerpt: The principal architect was probably Ahmad Lahori... a workforce of some 20,000 stone carvers, inlayers, and masons worked on the site.

facts.claim: Constructed using translucent Makrana white marble inlaid with semi-precious pietre dure gemstones from across Asia.
facts.sourceTitle: Archaeological Survey of India — Taj Mahal Records
facts.supportingExcerpt: The marble was quarried at Makrana in Rajasthan, complemented with lapis lazuli, turquoise, and jade.

images.caption: The ivory-white dome and minarets of the Taj Mahal at dawn.
